chapter_note: This chapter is overwhelmingly cosmological-architectural teaching (Living Spirit / Father of Life building and ordering the cosmos from the mixture), expressed through sustained correspondential metaphors (architect/carpenter) that remain inside the cosmic system. Only ¶1 contains an explicit dialogue-attribution frame formula; no NT citations or institutional/pastoral grafts appear despite the chapter-level fatigue warning.

paragraphs.core_text: At the time when the F[ir]st [Man ...] he gave the leadership to his five [sons ... the] Living Spirit and the Mother of Life [...] as the entire ruling-power is entwined and crucified [...] they were poured out and mixed with each other, the light with the darkness and the darkness with the light.
paragraphs.removed_material: Removed opening dialogue attribution frame: "[Once again] the enlightener [speaks]:"
paragraphs.temporal_note: The opening attribution (“the enlightener speaks”) is a classic later compilation frame, while the remaining sentence is impersonal cosmological mechanism (mixture of light/darkness; First Man; Living Spirit; Mother of Life) consistent with the older systematic teaching.

paragraphs.core_text: At that time the Living Spirit called one of his sons, one rich with power. He gave to him the leadership of the garments. Now, he himself [...] of [...] he hung them and set them up [...] of the Father of Life [...] he set up all things [...] he opened [...] ten firmaments [...] the wheel of the stars [...] them and the [...].
paragraphs.temporal_note: Pure cosmological narration/ordering: the Living Spirit appoints a son over the garments and establishes firmaments and the star-wheel. No audience address, citation formula, or institutional identification; the mapping stays within cosmic architecture.

paragraphs.core_text: ⟨p.132⟩ The Living Spirit is like this: Just as [...] and an architect who might build a dwelling for the king, and divide it up into separate houses and [separate ...] everything that is required for beauty [...] and he cleans them. And also the stones [...] them for beauty and {loveliness}, and he arranges them and makes them so that should the king come and inhabit that palace, he might glorify him.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Sustained correspondential simile (Living Spirit ↔ architect) used to describe cosmic construction; the referents remain archetypal (“king,” “palace”), not contemporary institutions—typical of the teaching substrate’s explanatory style.

paragraphs.core_text: Furthermore, the Father of Life resembles a wise and skilled carpenter [...] before it was worked [...] before it was established and made beautiful and [...] carpenter [...] works in it, but [...] in him in his [...] in his understanding, and he brings the saw and the adze, and cuts it into separate pieces [...] it and he pulls the [...] it with the {plane} and he smooths it. He shall make many [...] wooden implements, arranging them shape by shape; he cuts and produces wooden implements from it, wooden implements of different kinds, (such as) dishes, bowls. This wood, that [...] since previously it had not been worked before it was sealed by [the ski]ll and wisdom of this dextrous carpenter. He cut it up into different sorts of implements useful to his master.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Although flagged by vocabulary as ‘pastoral’ (likely due to verbs like “He shall make”), the paragraph is entirely third-person descriptive, extending the cosmic-building metaphor (Father of Life ↔ carpenter) without exhortation or church/institutional targets—best read as core teaching.

paragraphs.core_text: So is it also with the Father of Life. In his wisdom he has [...] in limbs [...] palace [...] in it or in a [...] useful [...] the ships of light [...] all the other works [...] in the [...] so that when the great king comes, he who is the Third Ambassador, who [...] he might dwell in this universe [...]
paragraphs.temporal_note: Explicit internal cosmological identification (Third Ambassador as “great king”; ships of light; universe as constructed dwelling). This is application of the metaphor back to the cosmic hierarchy, not to a community practice.

paragraphs.core_text: ⟨p.133⟩ ... live. The light, however, that is in it [...] wise, and he takes it up to the land; but the waste and the darkness will be gathered and thrown down to the abyss.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Cosmic sorting/eschatological mechanics (light gathered upward; darkness cast to abyss) stated impersonally, with no frame, citation, or pastoral address—consistent with the older mechanistic layer despite fragmentary preservation.
